newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus welcomes EU decision, slams Turkish warnings.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus welcomes EU decision, slams Turkish warnings.

text.p: Cyprus on Wednesday hailed the European Commission's committment to include it in its expansion talks and said the move could help in resolving the Cypriot problem.
But Nicosia criticised Ankara for warning it would integrate the northern part of the divided island to Turkey if negotiations do go ahead.

Acting president Spyros Kyprianou told Reuters membership in the bloc could assist in finding a solution to the protracted dispute splitting the eastern Mediterranean island, reiterating however that accession should not be held hostage to a solution of the conflict currently dividing Cyprus.

"I think it is a very positive decision on the part of the Commission because the membership of Cyprus in the European Community will no doubt contribute greatly to the proper solution of the Cyprus problem.

"Having said that it does not mean I support the idea that every effort for a solution must stop in the meantime. It will definitely be much better if we had a solution before the entry of Cyprus into the European Union but if we cannot succeed Cyprus should not be punished," said Kyprianou, president of Cyprus between 1977 and 1988.
On Tuesday Europe reaffirmed its committment to open accession talks with Cyprus, along with the Czech Republic, Poland, Hungary, Slovenia and Estonia, next year.

The Commission's decision sparked a swift response from Bulent Ecevit, Turkey's deputy prime minister. Ecevit said if the EU went ahead with planned membership talks with Cyprus, Turkey would have no choice but to unite with the northern third of the island.
"As far as the threats of Mr. Ecevit are concerned I think Europe and the United States have a duty and a responsibility to deal with these threats," Kyprianou said.

Ankara says allowing Cyprus to join before a solution on the divided island would be a one-sided move that ignored the wishes of the Turkish north and reinforced the current divisions between Greek and Turkish Cypriots.
Turkey occupied northern Cyprus in 1974 after a brief coup in Nicosia engineered by the military then ruling Athens.
The Greek Cypriot-led government in the south, is internationally recognised as the only government on the island. The breakaway state in the north, proclaimed in 1983, is recognised only by Ankara.
The Commission's decision comes a few days after United Nations-sponsored talks between the two sides aimed at re-uniting the island as a bi-communal, bizonal federation.
